rows.subtopic: Ageing parents' physical changes and how family responds
rows.description: A child sees a grandparent moving slowly, repeating or needing help, and may be curious, frightened or tender. Honest, simple explanations and shared activities teach respect and love for elders.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: affection, admiration, fear, curiosity

rows.subtopic: Ageing parents' physical changes and how family responds
rows.description: A young adult away at college hears that a parent is unwell and feels helpless and guilty about being far away. Regular calls, sharing tasks with siblings and visiting when possible ease the strain.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 23–26
related mind states: anxiety, guilt

rows.subtopic: Ageing parents' physical changes and how family responds
rows.subtype: Adult child noticing parents slowing down [Observer]
rows.description: An adult child sees a parent walk slower, hear less or tire faster, and feels a sudden wave of sadness and protectiveness. Seeing the ageing of the people who once cared for you is a quiet milestone.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22
related mind states: sadness

rows.subtopic: Ageing parents' physical changes and how family responds
rows.description: An older parent may refuse a walker, hearing aid or help at home because it feels like losing independence and dignity. The refusal is often fear of being a burden, not stubbornness.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22
related mind states: fear

rows.subtopic: Ageing parents' physical changes and how family responds
rows.description: A young adult caring for an ageing parent while working and raising a child feels love, duty and resentment together, with little rest. Sharing tasks, asking siblings and using outside help are responsible, not selfish.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22
related mind states: affection, resentment

rows.subtopic: Ageing parents' physical changes and how family responds
rows.description: A family talks with the parent, not over them, about what they want, adapts the home for safety and divides responsibilities fairly among siblings and in-laws. Listening and consistent kindness matter more than perfect solutions.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22
related mind states: admiration, trust

rows.subtype: Young person meeting a grandparent's forgetfulness [Observer]
rows.description: A student sees a grandparent forget names, repeat questions or get lost, and feels confusion, grief and sometimes impatience. Learning that this is illness, not carelessness, helps them respond gently.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 23–26
related mind states: grief, confusion

rows.description: A person with dementia may feel frightened, lost and sometimes angry, aware that something is wrong yet unable to explain it. They still feel love, embarrassment and dignity, and need to be treated as a person.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22
related mind states: affection, anger, fear, embarrassment

rows.description: Relatives may feel ambiguous grief as the person they know changes while still alive, along with guilt, exhaustion and moments of joy. Support groups, honest talk and shared care lessen the isolation.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22
related mind states: joy, grief, guilt, tiredness

rows.description: A caregiver hears the same question many times, feels patience thin and then feels guilty for it. Brief calm answers, gentle redirection and their own breaks are sustainable ways to keep kindness alive.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22
related mind states: guilt, calm
